title: Job 4:12–21
context: Job 4:12–21 continues the speech of Eliphaz, who describes a night vision. A word was secretly brought to him, fear and trembling seized him, a spirit passed before his face, and a voice asked whether a mortal can be more just than God or more pure than his Maker. If God puts no trust in his servants and charges his angels with error, how much less can humans, who live in houses of clay and are crushed like a moth, stand before him. Eliphaz presents this vision as the basis of his authority, but it is his report of what he heard, not the LORD’s verdict in the book. Both traditions affirm that no human being is righteous before God in his own strength, and both can say more about that truth from the rest of Scripture. They also note that Eliphaz uses it to imply that Job’s suffering proves guilt, a conclusion the book rejects (1:8; 42:7).

verses.text: “Now a thing was secretly brought to me. My ear received a whisper of it.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says a word was secretly brought to him, and his ear received a whisper of it. Arminians see him claiming a special revelation to support his argument, which gives his words a sense of authority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the claim as an attempt to strengthen his case. Both traditions note that the book does not confirm that this vision came from God, and they read it as Eliphaz’s report, not the LORD’s verdict.

verses.text: In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men,
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says it came in thoughts from night visions, when deep sleep falls on people. Arminian readers see the description of a dramatic experience, which Eliphaz uses to give weight to what follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as part of his account. Both traditions avoid treating the vision as authoritative simply because Eliphaz describes it vividly, and they let the book’s later verdict guide the reading.

verses.text: fear came on me, and trembling, which made all my bones shake.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says fear and trembling came on him and made his bones shake. Arminians see a vivid description of terror, which Eliphaz presents as evidence of the vision’s seriousness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as part of Eliphaz’s account. Both traditions note that intense experience alone does not confirm the source or the application of a message, and they read it as his report.

verses.text: Then a spirit passed before my face. The hair of my flesh stood up.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says a spirit passed before his face and the hair of his flesh stood up. Arminian readers see a mysterious experience that Eliphaz describes in frightening detail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The word translated spirit can also mean breath or wind, and both traditions avoid speculating about the nature of what Eliphaz saw, reading the verse as part of his account.

verses.text: It stood still, but I couldn’t discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes. Silence, then I heard a voice, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says the form stood still, he could not discern its appearance, and after silence he heard a voice. Arminians see the uncertainty of the vision, as Eliphaz cannot clearly describe what he saw.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the mystery of the scene. Both traditions read the verse as preparing for the message of the vision, which Eliphaz presents as authoritative but which remains his report.

verses.text: ‘Shall mortal man be more just than God? Shall a man be more pure than his Maker?
verses.arminianNotes: The voice asks whether a mortal can be more just than God, or more pure than his Maker. Arminian readers see a truth that both traditions affirm, that no human is righteous before God in his own strength, while noting that Eliphaz uses it to imply Job’s guilt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the claim is true in itself and connect it with Scripture’s wider teaching on human sin (compare Romans 3:23). Both traditions note that this is Eliphaz’s claim, not yet the LORD’s verdict, and that the book does not use it to explain Job’s suffering.

verses.text: Behold, he puts no trust in his servants. He charges his angels with error.
verses.arminianNotes: The voice says God puts no trust in his servants and charges his angels with error. Arminians see a statement of God’s absolute holiness, before which even heavenly beings fall short.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the contrast between the Creator and all creatures. Both traditions note that the statement is part of Eliphaz’s vision and should be read with caution, since the book does not confirm its source.

verses.text: How much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed before the moth!
verses.arminianNotes: The voice says that if this is true of angels, how much more of those who live in houses of clay, founded in dust, crushed like a moth. Arminian readers see a picture of human frailty and dependence on God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image of clay and dust as recalling humanity’s creation from the ground (Genesis 2:7). Both traditions affirm human frailty, while noting that Eliphaz uses it to diminish Job’s claims.

verses.text: Between morning and evening they are destroyed. They perish forever without any regarding it.
verses.arminianNotes: The voice says humans are destroyed between morning and evening and perish forever without anyone noticing. Arminians see a stark description of the brevity of human life, which is true in general.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the frailty of life as a reason for humility before God. Both traditions note that the vision speaks without hope, and they read it as Eliphaz’s report rather than the book’s final word.

verses.text: Isn’t their tent cord plucked up within them? They die, and that without wisdom.’
verses.arminianNotes: The voice asks whether their tent cord is not pulled up, so they die without wisdom. Arminian readers see the image of a tent collapsing as a picture of sudden death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as concluding the vision’s message about human frailty. Both traditions note that Eliphaz presents this as wisdom for Job, though the book will show it does not explain his suffering.
